bloecke.md:
A 401(k) is a retirement plan that an employer sets up under Section 401(k) of the Internal Revenue Code. You choose a percentage of your pay, which is deferred into your account before you receive it, and you choose the investments from the plan's menu. Public schools, hospitals and other nonprofits offer the very similar 403(b), state and local governments the 457(b), and the federal government and the military the Thrift Savings Plan (TSP). No employer is required by federal law to offer a plan, and you have no legal right to one. Several states have their own programs for employers without a plan.

The money is held in a trust, separate from the employer's assets, and the people who run the plan are fiduciaries under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA). If the employer goes bankrupt, the vested balance remains yours. Unlike a traditional pension, a 401(k) promises no particular benefit. You bear the investment risk, and the result depends on how much goes in, what it costs and how it is invested.

bloecke.md:
## Limits in 2026

The limit for your own elective deferrals to 401(k), 403(b) and TSP plans is $24,500 in 2026 (26 U.S.C. § 402(g)). It applies per person, not per plan, so two jobs in one year share it. From age 50, a catch-up contribution of $8,000 is allowed, and in the years in which you turn 60, 61, 62 or 63, a higher catch-up of $11,250. Your deferrals, the employer's money and any after-tax contributions together may not exceed $72,000 a year, or 100% of your pay (26 U.S.C. § 415(c)). Pay above $360,000 is disregarded for plan purposes.

Since 2026, employees whose Social Security wages from the employer exceeded the indexed threshold of $150,000 in the previous year must make catch-up contributions as Roth contributions. Regular deferrals can still be pre-tax.

bloecke.titel: Social Security and Medicare tax are not saved
bloecke.md: Pre-tax deferrals reduce federal income tax and, in most states, state income tax. They do not reduce Social Security and Medicare tax, which is paid on the full salary. The advantage is smaller than many expect, but it has a benefit: your Social Security record is not reduced, and the withdrawals in retirement are not subject to payroll tax.

What a deferral costs you in take-home pay therefore depends only on your marginal income tax rate. In the 22% federal bracket and a state without income tax, each dollar deferred costs 78 cents of take-home pay. In a state with income tax, the cost falls further. Roth deferrals reduce take-home pay dollar for dollar, because they come from taxed pay.

bloecke.titel: Net cost of a $250 monthly pre-tax deferral
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a 22% federal marginal tax rate and no state income tax. Social Security and Medicare tax remain unchanged.

bloecke.titel: Contribution per dollar of take-home pay forgone
bloecke.md:
An employee earns $60,000, $5,000 a month, and defers 5%, that is $250. Her take-home pay falls by $195. The employer matches 50% of deferrals up to 6% of pay and adds $125. Together, $375 goes into the account each month.

The ratio is 375 ÷ 195 = 1.92. One dollar of take-home pay becomes $1.92 in the account before any investment return. A taxable brokerage account funded from take-home pay first has to make up this head start. It is the main reason why a 401(k) with a match comes out ahead in almost every comparison.

## The employer match

A match is money the employer adds in proportion to your own deferral, up to a limit. You receive it only if you contribute yourself. Common formulas are 50% of deferrals up to 6% of pay, or 100% of the first 3% and 50% of the next 2%. The latter is the basic safe harbor formula, which spares the employer certain annual nondiscrimination tests and must vest immediately. Some employers match each paycheck separately. If you reach the annual limit early in the year, you can lose part of the match unless the plan makes a true-up at year end.

In practice, the match is the most important number in your plan. A dollar of match is an immediate return of 50% or 100% on your deferral, without investment risk. Not contributing enough to get the full match is the most common and most expensive mistake with a 401(k).

bloecke.md: Your own deferrals always belong to you. Employer contributions may be subject to a vesting schedule, under which you earn ownership with years of service. For matching contributions, the law allows at most a three-year cliff, under which nothing vests before three years and everything after, or a graded schedule reaching 100% after six years. If you leave earlier, the unvested part goes back to the plan. Safe harbor matches vest immediately.

bloecke.unter: The slowest schedules the law allows for matching contributions (26 U.S.C. § 411). Many employers vest faster; the plan's summary plan description states the schedule.

bloecke.md:
## Taxes and side effects in the payout phase

The tax saved in the accumulation phase is collected in the payout phase. Every dollar from the pre-tax part of a 401(k) is taxed as ordinary income at your marginal rate, federal and in most states. Withdrawals are not subject to Social Security or Medicare tax. Qualified withdrawals from a Roth 401(k) are tax-free, and since 2024, Roth accounts in employer plans have no required minimum distributions during the owner's lifetime.

The effects on other parts of your finances are less obvious. Withdrawals raise your provisional income and can make up to 85% of your Social Security benefits taxable. In the range where benefits are being phased into taxation, each additional dollar withdrawn makes 50 or 85 cents of benefits taxable as well. This raises the effective marginal rate on the withdrawal well above your bracket, an effect often called the tax torpedo. Higher income can also trigger the income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA) on Medicare premiums two years later, and before 65 it reduces premium tax credits for marketplace health insurance.

bloecke.md:
When you leave an employer, you can usually leave the money in the plan, roll it into the new employer's plan or an IRA, or take it in cash. Cashing out is expensive. Of a $20,000 balance, an employee in the 22% bracket under 55 loses $4,400 in income tax and $2,000 in additional tax, $6,400 in total, before state tax. The plan must also withhold 20% for federal tax if the money is paid to you.

A direct rollover avoids all of this. If you have an outstanding 401(k) loan, it usually becomes due when you leave. An unpaid balance is treated as a distribution unless you deposit the same amount in an IRA by your tax filing deadline, including extensions. Balances of up to $7,000 can be moved to an IRA by the plan without your consent, and smaller ones may be paid out.

## Effects on Social Security and other benefits

Because Social Security and Medicare tax is paid on deferred pay, a 401(k) does not reduce your Social Security record. Pre-tax deferrals do, however, lower your adjusted gross income. That can increase means-tested tax benefits, for example the Saver's Credit, premium tax credits for marketplace health insurance or a lower payment under an income-driven student loan plan. Roth deferrals do not have this effect.

If you leave your employer in or after the calendar year in which you turn 55, you can withdraw from that employer's 401(k) or 403(b) without the 10% additional tax. For public safety employees in governmental plans, the age is 50. The rule applies only to the plan of the employer you leave, not to IRAs and not to plans from earlier jobs. Rolling the money into an IRA before you need it can therefore cost you this exception until 59½.

## 401(k) or taxable brokerage account

A fair comparison starts from the same take-home pay forgone, not the same gross amount. $195 of take-home pay forgone a month results in a contribution of $375 to the 401(k) in the example with a 50% match, and an investment of $195 in a taxable brokerage account.

bloecke.md:
The calculation assumes a return of 5% a year and 300 monthly contributions for both variants. Fund costs are left out. The taxable account holds a stock index fund whose dividends are ignored for simplicity.

- The 401(k) reaches $375 × 595.5 (future value annuity factor) = around $223,300. After an assumed average income tax of 15% on withdrawals, around $189,800 remains.
- The taxable account reaches $195 × 595.5 = around $116,100, of which $58,500 are contributions and around $57,600 is gain. Long-term capital gains tax of 15% costs around $8,600. Around $107,500 remains.
- Without a match, the 401(k) reaches $250 × 595.5 = around $148,900, and around $126,500 after tax.

Calculated the other way round, the 401(k) with match only falls to the result of the taxable account if it earns less than 1% a year. The head start therefore absorbs about four percentage points of annual costs. Without a match, the break-even return is about 3.9%, so the plan may cost about one percentage point more a year than the taxable account before it falls behind.

Plan costs vary widely, from a few hundredths of a percent in large plans and the TSP to well over 1% a year in some small plans. The Department of Labor shows what this means in its guide to 401(k) fees: with a balance of $25,000, a return of 7% and 35 years without further contributions, fees of 0.5% a year leave around $227,000, fees of 1.5% only around $163,000. That is 28% less. Your plan must send you an annual fee disclosure. If the funds on offer are expensive, contribute enough to get the full match and use an IRA for further saving.

schritte.text: Find out the match formula and contribute at least the percentage needed for the full match. Ask whether the plan makes a true-up if you reach the annual limit early.
Before you change jobs, find out how much of the employer money is vested. A few months can decide whether you keep 60% or 100%.
A broad index fund or a low-cost target-date fund from the menu is usually enough. Compare the expense ratios in the fee disclosure.
In a low bracket, Roth deferrals are usually worth considering; in a high bracket, pre-tax deferrals. A mix keeps the choice open in retirement.

schritte.titel: Raise the rate with every raise
schritte.text: Increase the deferral by one percentage point a year or use automatic escalation, until you reach your savings target or the limit.
Anything beyond the match can go into a Roth or Traditional IRA, a health savings account or back into the 401(k), depending on costs and tax rate.

bloecke.md:
- **Automatic enrollment:** new 401(k) and 403(b) plans set up after 29 December 2022 must, from 2025, enroll employees automatically at 3% to 10% of pay and increase the rate by one point a year to at least 10%. Small and new employers, churches and governments are exempt. Employees can opt out.
- **Catch-up at 60 to 63:** since 2025, a higher catch-up limit applies in these years, $11,250 in 2026.
- **Roth catch-up for higher earners:** since 2026, catch-up contributions of employees with prior-year Social Security wages above $150,000 must be Roth contributions.
- **Roth employer contributions:** plans may allow matching contributions to be made as Roth contributions; they are then taxable income for the employee.
- **Student loan match:** since 2024, employers may treat qualified student loan payments as deferrals for the match.
- **Long-term part-time employees:** since 2025, employees with at least 500 hours in two consecutive years must be allowed to make deferrals.

The tax treatment of withdrawals and the effect on Social Security taxation remained unchanged.

Two points are often overlooked. The first is **costs over time**: a 401(k) with a match beats almost every alternative, but a plan without a match and with high fees can fall behind a low-cost IRA or taxable account. The second is **inflation**: a 401(k) balance is invested and can keep pace with inflation, but a traditional pension from a private employer usually pays a fixed nominal amount and loses [[Purchasing power|purchasing power]] every year. Only some public pensions have a cost-of-living adjustment.

mitnehmen: In the model case, $195 of take-home pay forgone becomes a contribution of $375 with a 50% match; this factor of around 1.9 is the main advantage of a 401(k) and absorbs about four percentage points of annual costs before a taxable account draws level.
In 2026, you can defer up to $24,500, plus $8,000 from age 50 or $11,250 at 60 to 63; the total including employer money is limited to $72,000.
Pre-tax deferrals reduce income tax but not Social Security and Medicare tax; your Social Security record is therefore not reduced.
Withdrawals are ordinary income; in the range where Social Security benefits become taxable, the effective rate can be far above the bracket, for example 40.7% in the 22% bracket.
The decision depends on three things: the match formula, the vesting schedule and the costs of the funds on offer.

begriffe.text: The part of your pay that you choose to have contributed to a 401(k), 403(b), 457(b) or TSP account, pre-tax or Roth. The limit is $24,500 in 2026, plus catch-up contributions from age 50.
Employer contribution in proportion to your own deferral, for example 50% of deferrals up to 6% of pay. You receive it only if you contribute yourself, and it may be subject to a vesting schedule.

Gradual acquisition of ownership of employer contributions with years of service. Your own deferrals are always 100% vested; matching contributions vest after at most three years (cliff) or six years (graded).

Plan design in which the employer makes a minimum contribution, for example 100% of the first 3% of pay and 50% of the next 2%, which vests immediately. In return, the plan is exempt from certain annual nondiscrimination tests.

Transfer of a balance from an employer plan to another plan or an IRA without tax. A direct rollover avoids the mandatory 20% withholding; with an indirect rollover, the money must be redeposited within 60 days.

Informal term for the high effective marginal tax rate in the income range where Social Security benefits are being phased into taxation, because each additional dollar of other income also makes 50 or 85 cents of benefits taxable.
